Being Active & Going Outdoors

From the couch to the outdoors: this story sparks the joy of movement — no performance pressure, just the plain happiness of running, climbing and romping.

A personalized picture book in which your child is the hero — and masters this challenge themselves. The first story is free.

Create This Story

“Just five more minutes” — and the five minutes in front of the screen effortlessly turn into fifty. Outside, the playground is waiting, the bike, the woods at the end of the street, but your child would rather stay seated. Many parents know this stubborn negotiation over every minute of fresh air, while a guilty feeling grows alongside it: too much screen time, too little movement, and the worry that this becomes a habit for life.

For children this age, movement isn't an extra on top of everyday life — it's a basic condition for how brain and body develop; balance, coordination, even concentration build substantially on free, wild movement. Yet this competes with the strong pull of screens, which deliver instant reward, while movement only becomes properly fun after the first few minutes. And some children pull back from movement because they've already developed an early fear of failing — of coming last in a race, of dropping the ball they can't catch.

A story can interrupt this pull toward stillness without moralizing. Through a character who would rather sit still at first and then discovers the sheer joy of running, climbing or balancing, your child experiences movement as something fun — not as a duty or a performance to be judged. Your child also sees the character hesitate at first and still get moving eventually, and carries that small nudge along internally before heading outside themselves.

In the personalized story, your child is the main character — with their own face on every page, discovering climbing at the playground, running through the woods, or the first wobbly balance on a bike, entirely without competition or a best time. The focus stays on the joy of movement itself, not on winning. The first story is free, so you can look through it together before the next “come on, let's go outside.”

For home: turn movement into a shared ritual rather than an announcement — a walk after dinner, a short bike ride before bedtime. Praise the joy of moving itself (“that was fun!”) rather than performance (“you were the fastest”) — this protects against performance pressure and withdrawal after a setback. Offer choice instead of obligation: climbing, dancing, ball games — not every child needs the same sport. And if your child consistently avoids movement, gets out of breath very quickly, or complains of ongoing pain, talk to your paediatrician to rule out a physical cause.

What your child learns

Joy of movement, stamina, coordination, self-confidence, healthy habits.

Recommended age

3-9 years

Frequently Asked Questions

How much screen time is too much at this age?

There's no single number that fits every family, but a useful check is whether screens regularly crowd out active play, sleep, or time outdoors rather than sitting alongside them. If active alternatives keep losing to the screen, it's worth building fixed windows for outdoor time into the daily routine.

My child says movement is boring — what can I do?

Movement often only becomes fun after the first few minutes, so short initial resistance is normal, not a real verdict. Offer variety rather than one fixed activity — climbing, dancing, ball games, water play — since “boring” often just means the wrong activity was tried, not that movement itself doesn't appeal.

Should I sign my child up for competitive sports?

Not necessarily, and certainly not before your child enjoys movement for its own sake. Early competitive pressure can turn a joyful activity into a source of anxiety about winning or losing. Free, unstructured play and non-competitive activities build the same physical foundations at this age.

How much movement does my child actually need each day?

Health guidelines for this age generally point toward at least an hour of varied physical activity daily, spread across the day rather than in one block. What matters most in practice is that it stays playful and varied — running, climbing, dancing — rather than a single measured exercise session.

When should movement reluctance be checked by a doctor?

If your child avoids all physical activity consistently, gets unusually out of breath for simple tasks, or complains of recurring pain during movement, it's worth ruling out a physical cause with your paediatrician rather than assuming it's just reluctance. Most cases turn out to be about motivation, but persistent physical signs deserve a check.
